samples.task_summary: Predict whether a person will move residence across U.S. states using ACS person-level attributes that are stable and broadly predictive.

scores.rationale: Age is a strong, portable predictor of mobility life stage.
Education captures life-course and economic stability, usually predictive across states.
Marital status relates to household stability but is only moderately useful and somewhat demographic.
Sex may weakly correlate with mobility patterns but is a sensitive shortcut with limited stable signal.
Disability can affect mobility constraints, though effects may vary and be partially proxy-like.
Parent employment status is mainly relevant for children and is weakly applicable for this task.
Citizenship can matter for mobility, but it is sensitive and may encode demographic or policy differences.
Military service is rare and context-specific, so it offers limited stable predictive value.
Ancestry is a weak proxy for geography and demographics rather than a direct mobility driver.
Nativity can affect migration propensity, but it is a sensitive demographic proxy with modest stable signal.
Household relationship is useful for life-stage and family-structure effects on moving.
Hearing difficulty may affect mobility constraints, but the signal is indirect and sensitive.
Vision difficulty can matter for mobility, though it is only a moderate and indirect predictor.
Cognitive difficulty may reduce mobility, but it is a sensitive health proxy with limited robustness.
Race often acts as a demographic/geographic proxy and should be downweighted for OOD stability.
Grandparent-care status is niche and household-structure specific, so it is only weakly useful.
Class of worker reflects job flexibility and relocation constraints, which are fairly portable.
Employment status is a strong, broadly stable indicator of current attachment to work and mobility.
Usual weekly hours worked proxy labor-market attachment and stability, with good cross-state portability.
Commute time is highly relevant to moving behavior and tends to generalize well as a mobility-related signal.
Income is a strong general predictor of moving capacity and housing search behavior, though somewhat state-sensitive.

samples.task_summary: Predict whether a person will have a residential move or mobility-related outcome in the ACS mobility task using stable demographic, household, and labor-market signals.

scores.rationale: Age is a strong, broadly stable predictor of mobility and life-stage constraints across states.
Education is generally predictive of mobility-related behavior and remains semantically meaningful across regions.
Marital status captures household structure and stability, but effects are indirect and somewhat demographic.
Sex may have weak residual signal, but it is a sensitive demographic shortcut with limited stable causal relevance.
Disability status can affect mobility constraints and is fairly stable, though it is sensitive and may interact with age.
Mostly defined for children, so it is sparse and not broadly useful for this adult mobility task.
Citizenship can correlate with mobility patterns, but it is a sensitive proxy for nativity and geography-linked population composition.
Military service is relatively rare and only weakly related to mobility in a stable way.
Ancestry is often a demographic proxy with limited direct predictive value and potential geographic shortcutting.
Nativity has some association with mobility and migration history, but it is also a sensitive proxy and not strongly causal.
Household relationship is a strong, stable indicator of family structure and housing context relevant to mobility.
Hearing difficulty can modestly affect mobility, but the signal is indirect and sensitive.
Vision difficulty can affect independence and mobility, though its predictive power is moderate and indirect.
Cognitive difficulty can matter for mobility and household stability, with some stable relevance despite sensitivity.
Race often captures structural differences, but it is a sensitive demographic shortcut and may not generalize robustly.
Grandparent-care status reflects household composition and caregiving burden, which can relate to mobility decisions.
Class of worker is a stable labor-market feature tied to job flexibility, commuting, and relocation constraints.
Employment status is strongly and broadly predictive of mobility-related outcomes through labor-market attachment.
Usual weekly hours worked is a stable proxy for labor intensity and attachment, relevant to mobility constraints.
Commute time is highly relevant to residential mobility and tends to be semantically predictive across states.
Income is a strong general predictor of housing and mobility capacity, though it can be noisy and context-dependent.

Household relationship strongly reflects family structure and moving incentives.
Hearing difficulty can affect independence and household transitions moderately.

Household relationship is fairly informative about family structure and move propensity.

Cognitive difficulty can affect independence and relocation likelihood, with moderate robustness.
Race is a sensitive demographic proxy and may encode structural and geographic artifacts rather than stable causality.

samples.task_summary: Predict whether a person in the ACS PUMS sample is likely to have moved residence, using person-level attributes that generalize across states.

scores.rationale: Age is a strong, broadly stable predictor of mobility across states.
Education is consistently related to mobility, though effects vary somewhat by labor market and region.
Marital status has some stable signal through household stability, but it is indirect and weaker.
Sex may capture small behavioral differences, but it is a weak and potentially shortcut-prone predictor.
Disability can affect moving likelihood via constraints, with fairly general but moderate predictive value.
Mostly defined for children and not a stable general predictor for this adult mobility task.
Citizenship can matter for mobility constraints, but it is sensitive and may proxy geography or immigration patterns.
Military service is rare and only weakly related to mobility in a stable way.
Ancestry is mostly a demographic proxy with limited direct and stable predictive value.
Nativity can affect mobility through migration history, but it is also a sensitive demographic shortcut.
Household relationship is a useful stable proxy for family structure and household stability.
Hearing difficulty has some general association with mobility constraints, but the effect is modest.
Vision difficulty is similarly relevant to mobility constraints and should generalize reasonably well.
Cognitive difficulty can affect relocation capacity and tends to be a stable but moderate predictor.
Race is highly sensitive and often acts as a proxy for structural and geographic differences rather than direct mobility signal.
Grandparent-care status can reflect household responsibilities that influence moving, but it is niche and unevenly prevalent.
Class of worker is fairly stable and informative because job flexibility and sector often affect moving behavior.
Employment status is a strong, general predictor of mobility through labor-market attachment and life-stage effects.
Usual hours worked captures work attachment and schedule rigidity, which are robustly related to moving.
Commute time is one of the most directly relevant and stable predictors of residential mobility.
Income is broadly predictive of mobility capacity and housing search behavior, though it can be noisy and state-dependent.
